title: Version control: commits, differences and undoing

questions.prompt: What is a commit?

choices.text: A promise from the programmer to finish the project by a certain date in the future
A saved snapshot of code with a message

questions.correct_answer: A saved snapshot of code with a message
questions.intro: VERSION CONTROL keeps a history of code changes. A popular tool for it is called Git. A COMMIT is a saved snapshot with a short message ("Fix average for empty list"). A DIFF (difference) shows what changed between versions: lines starting with "-" were removed and lines with "+" were added. REVERTING undoes a commit by adding a new commit with the opposite change; RESTORING returns files to how they were in a saved version. A good habit with AI help: COMMIT BEFORE accepting generated changes, so you can see exactly what the tool changed in the diff and undo it if it breaks something.

sections.skill: Compare version control with save points in a video game

questions.prompt: A game save is like what?
questions.intro: In many video games you can SAVE before a hard level. If things go badly, you LOAD the save and try again. Each save is like a commit: a snapshot you can return to. Comparing two saves to see what changed, such as items gained or lost, is like a diff. Loading an earlier save is like restoring files from a commit. Saving before letting someone else play your game is like committing before accepting AI changes.

sections.title: Apply it

questions.prompt: A diff from a tool edit shows changes to a settings file you did not ask about. What should you do?

choices.text: Accept everything, since tools only change files that were needed for the requested task

questions.intro: Commit messages should say what changed and why, so others (and future you) can understand the history. Small commits that each do one thing are easier to review and undo than one huge commit. Generated changes sometimes touch files you did not expect, such as settings or unrelated code; the diff reveals this. Never commit secrets like passwords, because version history keeps them even after you delete them from the latest version.

questions.prompt: Why prefer small commits?

choices.text: Because large commits are not allowed by any version control tool that exists today
They are easier to review and undo
Because small commits use more storage

questions.correct_answer: They are easier to review and undo
